title: The Project Nobody Owns Just Became Your Problem
author: Empathy Elevated
summary: This piece addresses a specific workplace pattern: a stalled, ambiguously-owned project resurfaces months later, and a conscientious 'high EQ' employee instinctively absorbs ownership of it before anyone has actually asked them to, simply because raising the visible gap feels indistinguishable from being responsible for closing it. The author's central distinction is between naming a problem and owning its solution -- arguing that asking 'who is actually leading this?' and treating silence itself as diagnostic information is a legitimate, complete response, not a dodge that still requires the noticer to step in. It frames the instinct to immediately populate a project-management tool with tasks as 'absorption' disguised as leadership, arguing that clarity about ownership is itself the first deliverable, prior to and separate from any plan or task list. The piece explicitly separates the emotional-intelligence move (naming the gap without assigning blame, since people simply slip on to-do lists) from a Stoic move (controlling only one's own response, questions, and presence, not the drift or who caused it), and closes by noting that AI can draft the status-update message but cannot substitute for the deliberate, in-the-room choice to either claim or decline ownership.
points: The essay's core reframe is that 'shared ownership' on an org chart often means no one is actually accountable in practice, so a stalled project's resurfacing exposes a gap between formal hierarchy (Workday) and who is really driving work day to day.

Asking 'who is leading this?' and receiving silence is treated as a complete, sufficient diagnostic response in itself -- the piece explicitly argues this does not obligate the person who asked to then become the owner by default.

Naming a stalled project is deliberately separated from an accountability conversation about blame; the piece argues that surfacing the gap does the necessary work without requiring anyone to be assigned fault for the drift.

AI is explicitly carved out as useful only for drafting the message, not for the actual leadership moment -- reading the room and choosing whether to break the silence and claim ownership -- which the piece treats as irreducibly human judgment.
quotes: High EQ professionals who are generally conscientious from the start want to see success, and may find themselves raising their hand to take the first leap. They carry the disproportionate load.
Re-engaging in the project vs. an accountability discussion are two separate things. Do not allow them to be.
Ask openly: who is leading the project? If it's met with silence, you have your answer.
The moment you ask instead of absorb, you've already done the Stoic move — separated what's yours from what isn't.

But it cannot handle how you hold yourself as you walk into the stakeholder meeting, the milliseconds you take to read the room, and the moment you open your mouth and proclaim yourself as the owner and break the silence.
Before a task list, before the status update, and before you say YES to owning something that was never directly yours, ask who is really leading. Name what is stuck. Let the silence be the answer.
